title: CSS Transitions
summary: **CSS transitions** smoothly animate a property from one value to another over time when that property changes (for example on :hover or via a toggled class) — the simplest way to add polished, performant motion without JavaScript.

subtopics.title: The four transition properties
subtopics.explanation: A transition is configured by four longhand properties: transition-property (which CSS property to animate, or all), transition-duration (how long, required for anything to be visible), transition-timing-function (the acceleration curve), and transition-delay (how long to wait before starting). Duration is the only one with no useful default — without it the change is instant.

subtopics.title: The transition shorthand
subtopics.explanation: transition combines all four longhands in one declaration: transition: <property> <duration> <timing-function> <delay>. The first time value parsed is duration, the second is delay. You can list multiple comma-separated transitions to give different properties different timings.

subtopics.title: What can and cannot animate
subtopics.explanation: Transitions only work on properties that have a defined, interpolatable intermediate value — colors, lengths, opacity, transforms, etc. Properties like display, and auto values (e.g. height: auto), are not animatable in the traditional model, which is why people animate max-height or use transforms instead. transitioning all animates every animatable property that changes.

subtopics.title: Timing functions
subtopics.explanation: The timing function shapes the rate of change across the duration. linear is constant speed; ease (default) starts slow, speeds up, then slows; ease-in accelerates, ease-out decelerates, ease-in-out does both. cubic-bezier(x1, y1, x2, y2) defines a fully custom curve, and steps(n) jumps in discrete frames.

subtopics.title: Triggering on :hover and state changes
subtopics.explanation: A transition runs whenever the property's computed value changes. The canonical trigger is :hover, but any state change works — :focus, :active, or a JS-toggled class. Put the transition on the BASE selector (not only on :hover) so the change animates both into and out of the state.

subtopics.title: Animate transform and opacity for performance
subtopics.explanation: transform and opacity are the cheapest properties to animate because the browser can handle them on the compositor (often the GPU) without recalculating layout or repainting. Animating layout properties like width, height, top, or margin triggers reflow on every frame and can cause jank. Prefer translate/scale over top/left/width.

subtopics.title: Transition vs animation
subtopics.explanation: A transition animates a one-shot change between two states and needs a trigger (a value change). A @keyframes animation can run on its own, loop, define many intermediate steps, and play without a state change. Reach for transitions for hover/focus/toggle effects; reach for animations for looping or multi-step motion.
subtopics.example:
/* transition: needs a trigger */
.box:hover { transform: scale(1.1); }

foundations.overview: CSS transitions let you interpolate a property's value over a span of time instead of snapping instantly when it changes. You declare which property to watch, how long the change should take, and the easing curve; the browser then animates between the old and new values whenever something (a hover, a focus, a toggled class) changes that property.
foundations.formalDefinition: A CSS transition is a mechanism that implicitly animates changes to CSS property values, interpolating between the start and end values over a specified duration using a timing function and optional delay.
foundations.whyItMatters: Motion communicates state and provides feedback — buttons that ease on hover, panels that slide, inputs that highlight on focus. Transitions deliver this with a single declaration, no JavaScript, and excellent performance when applied to transform/opacity.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a transition as a rule that says: 'whenever this property changes, don't jump — glide from the old value to the new one over N milliseconds along this curve.' The trigger is any change to that property's computed value.
foundations.browserPerspective: When a watched property changes, the browser starts a transition: it computes intermediate values each frame using the timing function. For transform and opacity it can run this on the compositor thread (often GPU-accelerated), skipping layout and paint; for layout properties it must reflow and repaint each frame.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Hover and focus states on buttons and links, expanding/collapsing menus, fading tooltips and modals in and out, color and shadow changes on cards, and animated form-field highlights are nearly all built with transitions.
foundations.businessImpact: Subtle, smooth motion makes a UI feel responsive and trustworthy, improving perceived quality and engagement; janky or absent feedback makes interactions feel broken.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Transitions remove the need for JavaScript animation loops for simple state changes, reducing code and bugs while keeping motion declarative and easy to tune.
foundations.performanceImpact: Animating transform and opacity is cheap and stays at 60fps; animating layout-affecting properties (width, height, top, margin) forces per-frame reflow and can drop frames on lower-end devices.
commonUseCases: Smooth :hover and :focus styling on buttons and links
Fading elements in and out by transitioning opacity
Sliding or scaling panels and menus with transform
Animated color, border, and box-shadow changes on cards

commonMisconceptions.myth: You can transition any CSS property.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Only animatable properties with interpolatable values transition; things like display and height: auto don't animate in the classic model.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Putting the transition only on :hover is enough.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Define the transition on the base selector so the change animates both on entering AND leaving the state; on :hover only, the reverse snaps instantly.

visualExplorer.title: How a transition runs frame by frame
visualExplorer.caption: Step through what the browser does when a watched property changes and a transition begins.

steps.title: 1. Base state
steps.description: The element sits at its starting value, e.g. background: #3b82f6, with a transition declared on the base selector.

steps.title: 2. Trigger
steps.description: A state change (hover, focus, or toggled class) gives the property a new computed value.

steps.title: 3. Interpolation begins
steps.description: Instead of snapping, the browser starts a transition over the duration, computing intermediate values via the timing function.

steps.title: 4. Easing applied
steps.description: Each frame's value follows the timing-function curve (ease, linear, cubic-bezier), shaping acceleration.

steps.title: 5. End state reached
steps.description: At the end of the duration the property holds its new value; reversing the state animates back the same way.

interactiveExamples.title: A button that eases on hover
interactiveExamples.explanation: The transition is declared on the base .btn so both entering and leaving the hover state animate smoothly.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A blue button whose background eases to a darker blue on hover and back when you leave.

interactiveExamples.title: Lift and fade a card
interactiveExamples.explanation: Transitioning transform and opacity keeps the motion on the compositor for a buttery 60fps lift effect.
interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A card that smoothly lifts up with a deeper shadow on hover.

codeLab.title: Make a link underline grow in
codeLab.instructions: Add a transition so the link's underline (built with a scaled pseudo-element) smoothly grows from the left on hover instead of snapping. Hint: transition the transform property and use transform-origin.
codeLab.expectedOutput: The underline grows smoothly from the left on hover and shrinks back on leave.
hints: The underline animates because scaleX changes from 0 to 1 — add a transition on the transform property.
transform-origin: left makes the scale grow from the left edge rather than the center.

debuggingLab.title: The hover-out snaps instead of animating
debuggingLab.symptom: The button animates smoothly when you hover ON, but snaps back instantly when you move the mouse away.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The transition is declared only on .btn:hover, so it only applies while the element is hovered — that animates the change INTO the state. When you leave, the element reverts to .btn which has no transition, so the reverse change is instant.
commonMistakes: Declaring the transition on the :hover selector instead of the base selector.
Assuming a transition is 'attached' to an event rather than to a property's value change.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move the transition declaration to the base .btn selector so both directions animate.

theory.question: What is a CSS transition and what are its four properties?
theory.directAnswer: A CSS transition smoothly interpolates a property's value between two states over time when that property changes. It is configured by four properties: transition-property (what to animate), transition-duration (how long), transition-timing-function (the easing curve), and transition-delay (how long to wait before starting).

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: An implicit animation that runs whenever a watched, animatable property changes its computed value.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To add motion and feedback to state changes declaratively, without JavaScript animation loops.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: You declare the property, duration, timing function, and delay (often via the transition shorthand); when the value changes, the browser interpolates frame by frame.

theory.whyImportant: Transitions are the foundation of polished UI feedback and a very common CSS interview topic.
theory.realWorldExample: A button with transition: background 200ms ease eases its color on hover instead of snapping.

nestedTopics.title: transition-duration
nestedTopics.explanation: The only property with no useful default — without it the change is instant.

nestedTopics.title: transition shorthand
nestedTopics.explanation: Combines property, duration, timing-function, and delay in one declaration.

nestedTopics.title: Trigger
nestedTopics.explanation: A transition runs on any change to the property's value, e.g. :hover, :focus, or a toggled class.

followUps.question: Why should the transition go on the base selector, not :hover?
followUps.answer: So the change animates both into AND out of the state; if it's only on :hover, the reverse snaps instantly.

followUps.question: Which two time values does the shorthand parse, and in what order?
followUps.answer: The first time value is the duration, the second is the delay.

theory.question: Which CSS properties are cheap to animate and why?
theory.directAnswer: transform and opacity are the cheapest to animate because the browser can handle them on the compositor thread (frequently GPU-accelerated) without recalculating layout or repainting. Animating layout-affecting properties like width, height, top, or margin forces a reflow and repaint on every frame, which can cause jank.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A distinction between compositor-only properties (transform, opacity) and layout/paint-triggering properties.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Modern browsers split rendering into layout, paint, and composite stages; only composite is cheap to do per frame.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Changing transform/opacity skips layout and paint and just re-composites layers; changing width/top re-runs layout for every animated frame.

theory.whyImportant: Knowing this is the difference between 60fps motion and visible stutter, especially on mobile.
theory.realWorldExample: Use transform: translateY(-6px) instead of top: -6px to lift a card without triggering reflow.

nestedTopics.title: Compositor thread
nestedTopics.explanation: transform and opacity can be animated off the main thread for smoothness.

nestedTopics.title: Reflow
nestedTopics.explanation: Animating width/height/top recomputes geometry each frame.

nestedTopics.title: will-change
nestedTopics.explanation: Hints the browser to promote an element to its own layer, used sparingly.

followUps.question: How would you move an element smoothly without using top/left?
followUps.answer: Use transform: translate(x, y), which the compositor can animate without reflow.

scenario.question: A dropdown menu won't animate its open/close when you toggle display: none/block. Why, and how do you make it animate?
scenario.directAnswer: display is not an animatable property, so there's nothing to interpolate between none and block — the change is instant. To animate, keep the element in the layout and transition animatable properties instead: fade with opacity and move with transform, optionally toggling visibility (and pointer-events) rather than display.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A limitation of the classic transition model around non-animatable properties.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: display has discrete values with no meaningful intermediate states, so it can't be interpolated.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Transition opacity (1 to 0) and transform (e.g. translateY), and switch visibility/pointer-events to remove it from interaction after fading.

scenario.whyImportant: Animating show/hide correctly is a frequent real-world UI requirement.

nestedTopics.title: Non-animatable properties
nestedTopics.explanation: display and height: auto don't transition in the classic model.

nestedTopics.title: opacity + visibility
nestedTopics.explanation: Fade with opacity, then toggle visibility so it leaves the accessibility/interaction tree.

followUps.question: How do you animate an element to height: auto?
followUps.answer: Transition max-height to a large value, animate a grid-template-rows trick, or use the modern interpolate-size/calc-size where supported, since height: auto isn't directly animatable.

coding.question: Write CSS for a button that smoothly scales up and darkens on hover, with motion on both enter and leave.
coding.thoughtProcess: Put the transition on the base selector so both directions animate. Animate transform (scale) and background for cheap, smooth motion, and use an easing curve like ease-out for a natural feel.
coding.lineByLine: The transition is on .btn so entering and leaving hover both animate. transform: scale(1.05) grows the button via the compositor (no reflow), and background darkens. ease-out decelerates for a natural settle. On :hover the new values trigger the interpolation.

alternativeApproaches.title: Single shorthand on all
alternativeApproaches.explanation: transition: all 200ms ease animates every changed property, but is less explicit and can animate unintended properties.

followUps.question: Why scale instead of changing width/height?
followUps.answer: scale is a transform handled by the compositor with no reflow, so it stays smooth; width/height changes force layout each frame.

productionDeepDive.architecture: In design systems, transitions are encoded as tokens — standard durations (e.g. 150ms, 250ms) and easing curves (a shared cubic-bezier) — applied via utility classes or component styles so motion feels consistent across the product.
productionDeepDive.performance: Restrict animated properties to transform and opacity to stay on the compositor and hit 60fps. Avoid transition: all in hot paths, since it can animate expensive layout properties unintentionally; use will-change sparingly and remove it after the animation.
productionDeepDive.security: Motion has no direct security surface, but excessive or auto-playing motion can harm accessibility; respect user preferences and avoid using motion to obscure UI in ways that could mislead.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Centralize duration/easing tokens so hundreds of components share one motion language; this keeps timing coherent and makes global tuning a one-line change.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Always declare transitions on the base selector and prefer explicit property lists over all so future edits don't accidentally animate new properties.
productionDeepDive.observability: Browser DevTools' Performance panel and the animations inspector let you scrub transitions, see dropped frames, and confirm whether motion runs on the compositor.

caseStudies.problem: Inconsistent, sometimes janky motion across components.
caseStudies.solution: Shared motion tokens (durations + easing) and a rule to animate only transform/opacity.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Less per-component freedom in exchange for consistency and performance.
caseStudies.lessons: A small, shared motion vocabulary makes a product feel cohesive and fast.

projectBuilder.summary: Use transitions to give a product card lively, performant hover feedback: lift, image zoom, and an animated 'Add to cart' button.
requirements: A card that lifts with transform and deeper shadow on hover
An image that zooms slightly within a clipped container on hover
A button that scales and changes color smoothly on hover and focus
projectBuilder.architecture: Transitions declared on base selectors for .card, .card img, and .btn, animating only transform/opacity/box-shadow/background with shared 200ms ease-out timing.

steps.title: Card lift
steps.instructions: Add transition: transform 200ms ease-out, box-shadow 200ms ease-out and translateY(-6px) on hover.
steps.checkpoint: The card lifts smoothly and settles on leave.

steps.title: Image zoom
steps.instructions: Wrap the image in overflow: hidden and transition transform; scale(1.08) on hover.
steps.checkpoint: The image zooms within its frame without overflowing.

steps.title: Button feedback
steps.instructions: Transition transform and background on the base .btn; scale and darken on :hover and :focus-visible.
steps.checkpoint: The button responds on both hover and keyboard focus.

enhancements: Add prefers-reduced-motion to disable transitions for users who request it
Tune the easing with a custom cubic-bezier for a snappier feel
interviewQuestions: Why are the transitions on the base selectors rather than :hover?
Why animate transform/opacity instead of width/top for the lift and zoom?

keyTakeaways: A transition interpolates an animatable property between two states over a duration with a timing function and optional delay.
The transition shorthand is: property duration timing-function delay; the first time value is duration, the second is delay.
Declare transitions on the base selector so the change animates both into and out of a state like :hover.
Only animatable properties transition — display and height: auto don't; animate opacity/transform/max-height instead.
Animate transform and opacity for 60fps compositor-driven motion; avoid animating width, height, top, and margin.
